subject: Privacy & Digital Rights
title: The One-Time Pad
description: A 60-second lesson on The One-Time Pad.

hook.text: There's one encryption method that is mathematically impossible to break. It's called the one-time pad.

buildup.text: A one-time pad uses a random key as long as the message. Each key is used once and then destroyed.

discovery.text: Claude Shannon proved in 1949 that if the key is truly random and never reused, the cipher is unbreakable.

twist.text: The problem: sharing a key as long as every message is impractical. The perfect cipher is nearly unusable.

climax.text: The one-time pad proves that perfect secrecy exists — but convenience always wins over perfection.

punchline.text: Unbreakable by math. Impractical by reality.

quiz.question: Why is the one-time pad considered unbreakable?
options: The key is random, as long as the message, and never reused
It uses quantum computing to generate keys
It encrypts the message multiple times
